IGNITE-AI

Predictive Fire Safety Analytics for Space Station Orbit & Rocket Transit

IGNITE-AI is an open-source (Apache-2.0) tool that predicts whether a flame will spread over a spacecraft material under given oxygen, pressure, airflow and gravity conditions, using only published NASA experiments. It refuses to predict outside the conditions that were actually tested, shows the nearest real experiments with verbatim quotes, and answers questions from a NASA combustion knowledge base with citations.

[ Explore Space Fire Safety Tool ]

The Microgravity Fire Crisis

Fire changes character when gravity is removed. On Earth, hot gases rise and cooler air is pulled in at the base, which gives the familiar flickering teardrop flame. In the free fall of orbit that buoyant flow disappears: “low-momentum flames tend to be rounded or even spherical” (NASA). Near-limit flames can be very hard to see: in NASA tests at low airflow “the entire flame is pale violet and nearly invisible” (NASA/TM-2000-210337), and the FLEX experiment found cool flames in which fuel kept “burning” after the visible flame went out (NASA).

Pages

  • 3D Flame Simulator: Interactive 3D flame for Earth, Moon, Mars, ISS and transit-cabin conditions with sourced environment data and oxygen, pressure and airflow sliders.
  • Prediction & Experiments: Flame-spread prediction with a range guard, decision boundary over real NASA tests, nearest experiments and FLEX CO2 data.
  • Ask IGNITE-AI: Local question answering over a NASA combustion knowledge base; answers are verbatim quotes with source links.
  • Safety Measures: Spacecraft fire detection, ventilation shutdown, suppression, material selection and crew procedures from NASA sources.
  • Data & Model: The 144-row NASA flame-spread dataset with quotes and the honest model card: cross-validation, per-gravity accuracy, confusion matrix.
  • Sources & Citations: NASA PSI investigations, NTRS reports, environment and safety sources, FLEX data, and the AI-use disclosure.

Key numbers

  • 144 real NASA flame-spread experiments from 13 reports
  • 4 gravity levels with data (0, 0.165, 0.38, 1 g)
  • Cross-validated accuracy 0.729 vs majority baseline 0.611
  • 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations in the knowledge base

3D Flame Simulator

Interactive 3D flame for Earth, Moon, Mars, ISS and transit-cabin conditions with sourced environment data and oxygen, pressure and airflow sliders.

The 3D view is an illustrative rendering driven by the inputs and the model output (flame shape from √g buoyancy scaling, size and colour from O2 and pressure, skew from airflow). It is not a combustion simulation. Environment tabs: Earth (1 g), Moon (0.165 g), Mars (0.38 g), ISS microgravity (~0 g) and a transit cabin (coasting spaceflight is free fall; powered-flight thrust phases are not modelled).

Environments

Earth (1 g)

Buoyancy drives the classic flickering teardrop flame.

  • Gravity: 1 g (reference).
  • Reference atmosphere: Air: 21% O₂ / 79% N₂ at 14.7 psia (101.3 kPa). “normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)” — source: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Why flames are teardrops: Hot gas rises, cool air is pulled in at the base. “on Earth, hot gases from a flame rise and gravity pulls cooler, denser air to the bottom of a flame, creating the classic shape and flickering effect.” — source: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office
  • NASA material screening: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1: upward burning, pass/fail at 6 in (15 cm). “NASA STD 6001 Test 1 is the major method used to assess flammability of materials ... Materials that do not self-extinguish after six inches of burning must undergo other special considerations” — source: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)

Training data at this gravity: 6 real experiments. 6 training rows at 1 g: the upward limiting-oxygen (ULOI / MOC) tests for Mylar G, Ultem 1000 and Nomex HT90-40 at NASA White Sands (NTRS 20130010991 Table I). No 1 g rows exist for the other materials, so the range guard refuses them in this tab.

Moon (0.165 g)

Weak buoyancy: lunar gravity may be close to the MOST flammable condition.

  • Gravity: 0.165 g (1.62 m/s²). “For the Moon, the gravitational level is 1.62 m/s2, or 0.165 that of normal gravity.” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Planned habitat atmosphere: 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa), 34% O₂ / 66% N₂; control bands up to 37% O₂. “HLS, Lunar habitat and pressurized rover will nominally use 8.2 psia / 34% O2, 66% N2 ... Control bands are expected to allow up to 37% O2” — source: Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966)
  • Flammability at lunar g: Near the most flammable gravity level. “Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.” — source: Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966)
  • Partial-gravity maximum: Flammability peaks roughly between 0.15 and 0.4 g. “the partial-gravity fire maxima occur roughly over the range bracketing the levels of concern for missions beyond Earth orbit, namely, 0.15 to 0.4 of normal gravity.” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • First long-duration lunar-g burns: LUCI: >25 s burns on a spinning New Shepard rocket. “These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.” — source: Ferkul et al. (2025) Lunar Combustion Investigation (LUCI): Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket (NTRS 20250010653)
  • Buoyant flow speed vs Earth: ≈ 0.41 × Earth (√0.165) (ESTIMATE, not a measurement). Physics-based ESTIMATE: buoyant velocity scales as √(g·β·ΔT·L), so at fixed flame size and temperature it scales with √g. Not a measurement.

Training data at this gravity: 8 real experiments. 8 training rows at lunar g: ULOI*/MOC* for Mylar, Ultem, Nomex (drop-tower centrifuge, NTRS 20130010991) and 2 SIBAL downward-spread tests (parabolic flight, NTRS 20260001966; LUCI rocket, NTRS 20250010653). Low-g drop tests last only ~5 s.

Mars (0.38 g)

Martian gravity: limits measured up to 5.75 points of O₂ below Earth's.

  • Gravity: 0.380 g (3.72 m/s²). “For Mars, this "partial gravity" level is 3.72 m/s2, or 0.380 that of normal gravity.” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Habitat atmosphere: Not yet baselined in our sources; NASA-considered exploration atmospheres include 10.2 psia / 26.5% O₂ and 8.2 psia / 34% O₂. “NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.” — source: NASA PSI-20 ACME Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) investigation metadata
  • Measured Martian-g limits: Up to 5.75% O₂ lower than 1 g, typically between 1 g and lunar values. “The limiting oxygen levels at Martian gravity were significantly lower than normal gravity (up to 5.75% O2 lower), and typically between the normal gravity and Lunar gravity values.” — source: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Implication for screening: 1 g tests may not be conservative. “normal gravity material flammability screening tests may not be conservative and some materials tested to be safe for use in space may actually be flammable.” — source: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Buoyant flow speed vs Earth: ≈ 0.62 × Earth (√0.38) (ESTIMATE, not a measurement). Physics-based ESTIMATE from √g scaling of buoyant velocity. Not a measurement.

Training data at this gravity: 6 real experiments. 6 training rows at Martian g: ULOI*/MOC* for Mylar G, Ultem 1000 and Nomex HT90-40 (5.18 s drop-tower centrifuge, NTRS 20130010991 Table I). Every other material is refused in this tab.

ISS µg (~0 g)

No buoyancy: only ventilation and diffusion feed the flame.

  • Gravity: ~0 g (continuous free fall). — source: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office
  • Cabin atmosphere: Air, 21% O₂ at 14.7 psia (101.3 kPa). “the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have operated at normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)” — source: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Pre-EVA atmosphere: 30% O₂ at 10.2 psia (70.3 kPa). “brief pre-EVA activities when oxygen levels are increased for a short period of time to 30% oxygen while the total pressure is lowered to 10.2 psia” — source: Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Flame shape: Rounded or even spherical. “In microgravity, this flow doesn't occur and on the space station, low-momentum flames tend to be rounded or even spherical.” — source: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office
  • Role of ventilation: Flames spread poorly in still air, vigorously in flows up to ~20 cm/s. “Flames propagate poorly in truly quiescent conditions, but they are enhanced vigorously by low-rate atmospheric flows (velocities up to about 20 cm/s).” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Hard-to-see flames: At very low airflow a flame can be pale violet and nearly invisible. “At 1.0 cm/s, the entire flame is pale violet and nearly invisible” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Invisible cool flames: FLEX found fuel still 'burning' after the visible flame went out. “FLEX ... led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued “burning” under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.” — source: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office

Training data at this gravity: 124 real experiments. 124 training rows in microgravity: NASA drop towers, Shuttle SSCE, ISS BASS/BASS-II (corroborated by the PSI-25 experimental table) and Saffire I-VI in Cygnus.

Transit cabin (µg coast)

Coasting to the Moon or Mars is free fall: the same physics as the ISS.

  • Gravity while coasting: ~0 g, identical to orbit. “the environment in the transit phases of these journeys is microgravity, identical to the environment of Earth-orbiting spacecraft.” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Why transit is harder: Limited suppressant, delayed help from Earth. “Stores of suppressant and atmospheric diluents are more limited ... and consultation and emergency communications with Earth controllers may be of poor quality and delayed.” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Real spacecraft-cabin fires: Saffire burned large samples inside uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft. “Saffire is a series of experiments conducted aboard uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft after they depart the station” — source: NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office
  • Exploration atmospheres: Reduced pressure with higher O₂ (e.g. 8.2 psia / 34%). “10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.” — source: NASA PSI-20 ACME Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) investigation metadata
  • Powered flight: Most of the trip is unpowered; brief engine burns are not modelled. “practical travel to the Moon or Mars must assume flight, for the most part, that is unpowered and without artificial gravity.” — source: Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278) During engine burns the crew feels thrust acceleration instead of free fall; no flame-spread data exist for that, so the tool models the coast phase only.

Training data at this gravity: 124 real experiments. Uses the 124 microgravity rows; the Saffire (Cygnus spacecraft) rows are the closest real analogue to a crew-cabin fire in transit.

Outside these boxes, for untested gravity levels, or for gas mixes other than O2/N2, the tool refuses to predict.

Model and data

  • Dataset: 144 real flame-spread experiments transcribed from 13 NASA reports (NTRS), each with a verbatim quote and page reference; by gravity: 0 g: 124, 0.165 g: 8, 0.38 g: 6, 1 g: 6.
  • Model: sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.1); features oxygen_pct, pressure_kpa, flow_cm_s, gravity_g, material, flow_direction.
  • Stratified 5-fold cross-validated accuracy 0.729 (balanced 0.646); repeated CV 0.725 ± 0.064; leave-reports-out 0.688; majority-class baseline 0.611.
  • Out-of-fold accuracy by gravity: 0 g 0.798 (n=124), 0.165 g 0.375 (n=8), 0.38 g 0.333 (n=6), 1 g 0.167 (n=6). Partial-gravity outputs rest on very few tests and are effectively lookups of the nearest published test.
  • Confusion matrix (out-of-fold; rows = true no_spread, marginal_spread, spread): [[13, 5, 14], [6, 16, 2], [10, 2, 76]].
  • Range guard: no prediction is returned for a material/gravity combination, oxygen, pressure, airflow or flow direction outside the tested envelope, or for gas mixes other than O2/N2.
  • Separate real dataset: FLEX (PSI-69) experimental table, 274 droplet-combustion tests, 123 with added CO2 — shown as published, not used by the classifier.
  • Ask IGNITE-AI: retrieval over 1501 passages (NTRS abstracts, PSI metadata and tables, experiment rows, NASA pages) with TF-IDF; answers are verbatim quotes with source links; declines when nothing relevant is found.

Ask IGNITE-AI

Local question answering over a NASA combustion knowledge base; answers are verbatim quotes with source links.

How Ask IGNITE-AI works

Retrieval: TF-IDF (1–2-grams) over the knowledge base with a small fixed synonym list and at most three passages per source. Answer: the best-matching sentences shown verbatim with numbered citation links; lines built from real table rows are marked DATA; naming two or more investigations gives a side-by-side comparison from PSI metadata. It declines when the best match scores below 0.07, the question has no fire or space term, or fewer than 60% of the question's specific words appear in the retrieved passages.

Example: Is lunar gravity more flammable than Earth?

  • “The main hypothesis is that some materials burning in Lunar-g are more flammable than on Earth.” [2]
  • “Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.” [1]
  • “These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.” [3]
  • “Multiple fuel samples are to be individually burned in Lunar gravity, with cameras and other sensors recording flame characteristics.” [4]

Sources: [1] Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966); [2] NTRS 20210020516: Fire on the Moon: Solid Fuel Combustion Experiments; [3] Ferkul et al. (2025) Lunar Combustion Investigation (LUCI): Flammability Results from a Rotating Sounding Rocket (NTRS 20250010653); [4] NTRS 20210020516: Fire on the Moon: Solid Fuel Combustion Experiments

Example: How do flames look in microgravity?

  • “In microgravity, this flow doesn't occur and on the space station, low-momentum flames tend to be rounded or even spherical.” [1]
  • “FLEX ... led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued “burning” under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.” [2]
  • “Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction.” [3]
  • “Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4.” [3]

Sources: [1] NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office; [2] NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office; [3] NASA PSI PSI-10: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design (ACME/Flame Design)

Example: What does the crew do when a fire alarm goes off on the ISS?

  • “Upon a verified fire alarm, the automated or manual crew response is to isolate the affected zone, removing power and local or general air circulation.” [1]
  • “This raises new scientific questions about soot processes as well as practical issues for particulate size sensitivity and detection alarm threshold levels used in on-orbit smoke detectors.” [4]
  • “The fire response respirator cartridge does not filter carbon dioxide (CO2)” [2]
  • “The fire response respirator cartridge does not filter carbon dioxide (CO2), so a crew member discharging a CO2 fire extinguisher while wearing this filtering respirator would be at risk of inhaling unsafe levels of CO2.” [3]

Sources: [1] Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278); [2] Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300); [3] NTRS 20110012300: Development of the International Space Station (ISS) Fine Water Mist (FWM) Portable Fire Extinguisher; [4] NTRS 19970020580: Comparative Soot Diagnostics: Preliminary Results

Safety Measures

Spacecraft fire detection, ventilation shutdown, suppression, material selection and crew procedures from NASA sources.

Fire safety measures

Detection (applies to: earth, moon, mars, iss, transit)

  • ISS smoke detectors: Photoelectric smoke detectors in each module, as spot or duct monitors. “segments of the International Space Station (ISS) will have one or more detector units in each module that sense smoke through photoelectric light-beam obscuration and scattering” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Confirm with gas sensing: Combined CO/CO₂ sensing can tell flaming from non-flaming events. “combined CO/CO 2 detectors are shown in ground tests to discriminate among non-flaming fires, flaming fires, and non-fire events.” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Don't rely on seeing flames: Low-flow microgravity flames can be nearly invisible; FLEX cool flames kept 'burning' after the visible flame went out. “FLEX ... led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued “burning” under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.” — NASA (2023) Studying Combustion and Fire Safety - Space Station Research Integration Office
  • Orion: Orion's smoke detector is adapted from a mature commercial-aircraft design. “The smoke detector described in this paper is an adaptation of a mature commercial aircraft design for manned spaceflight.” — Smoke Detection for the Orion Crew Exploration Vehicle (2009, NTRS 20090020655)

Ventilation shutdown & isolation (applies to: iss, transit, moon, mars, earth)

  • First response: Isolate the zone: remove power and air circulation. “Upon a verified fire alarm, the automated or manual crew response is to isolate the affected zone, removing power and local or general air circulation.” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Necessary, not sufficient: Stopping airflow may not put out every fire (a candle on Mir burned for minutes). “removal of air flow upon fire detection is a necessary response, but it is not always sufficient for control of the incipient fire.” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Saffire lesson: Charring or bubbling materials may not self-extinguish quickly in still air. “Extinguishment of thin charring fuels at increased oxygen cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions.” — Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)
  • Saffire lesson: A small residual flow can sometimes help extinction. “In some circumstances, reducing air flow to a small value rather than quiescent conditions may be useful to disperse fuel vapor and help cool the material to enable extinction” — Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

Suppression (applies to: iss, transit, moon, mars, earth)

  • ISS extinguishers: CO₂ in the US segment, Columbus and Kibo; water foam in the Russian segment. “The International Space Station presently uses two different types of fire extinguishers: a water foam extinguisher in the Russian Segment, and a carbon dioxide extinguisher in the US Segment and Columbus and Kibo pressurized elements.” — Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300)
  • Why water mist: Fine water mist avoids filling the cabin with CO₂ and low-O₂ air. “Fine Water Mist extinguishes a fire without creating a large volume of air with reduced oxygen and elevated CO2.” — Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300)
  • Crew breathing: Fire-response respirator cartridge rated up to 90 min; it does not filter CO₂. “It is qualified to provide up to 90 minutes of capability ... The fire response respirator cartridge does not filter carbon dioxide (CO2)” — Development of the ISS Fine Water Mist Portable Fire Extinguisher (2011, NTRS 20110012300)
  • Orion: Orion uses a water-spray portable extinguisher. “The Orion crew capsule will utilize a different PFE technology from ISS (water spray rather than water mist)” — Orion Portable Fire Extinguisher Performance Testing ... (2018, NTRS 20180005251)
  • Depressurization: If used, drop the pressure fast. “if a fire is to be controlled by depressurization, the pressure in the affected module should be decreased rapidly” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

Material selection (applies to: earth, moon, mars, iss, transit)

  • Standard test: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1: upward burning in the worst expected atmosphere. “The method is a pass/fail upward flame propagation test conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft” — Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Low-g margin: Some materials burn at lower O₂ in low g than in 1 g. “1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials as evidenced by the negative ∆O2%, by up to -5.75% oxygen.” — Olson & Ferkul (2012) Evaluating Material Flammability in Microgravity and Martian Gravity Compared to the NASA Standard Normal Gravity Test (NTRS 20130010991)
  • Higher O₂ habitats: Fire-safe materials get harder to find as O₂ rises. “Fire safe materials become increasingly difficult to find as the oxygen concentration increases.” — Ferkul et al. (2026) Material Flammability at Lunar and Martian Gravity, LPSC presentation (NTRS 20260001966)
  • Saffire lesson: Thick-fuel growth in low g differs from Test 1. “Thick fuel flame growth was found to be dissimilar from that seen in NASA STD 6001 Test 1. This does not invalidate the test but does affect the interpretation of the test results” — Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

Crew procedures & post-fire (applies to: iss, transit, moon, mars, earth)

  • Re-ignition: Hot embers can re-ignite if fresh air returns too early. “Since burned material remains hot in the non-convective environment, embers may reignite if prematurely exposed to fresh air.” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • Deflagration risk: Overheated materials in still zones can build up fuel vapour. “Overheated materials in quiescent conditions or in low-flow zones in low gravity can produce stratified fuel mixtures that can result in dramatic deflagrations during ignition.” — Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)
  • Flame jumps: A flame jumped a 4.5 cm gap to a warmed PMMA surface. “In one case, a flame was seen to jump a 4.5 cm gap to ignite a previously warmed PMMA surface.” — Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)
  • Large fire impact: Saffire fires up to 10 kW did not push average vehicle conditions to unacceptable levels. “despite having heat release rates up to 10 kW, the average vehicle conditions did not rise to unacceptable levels.” — Urban et al. (2021) Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V, ICES-2021-266 (NTRS 20210011521)

Moon & Mars specifics (applies to: moon, mars)

  • Most flammable band: Flammability and spread rate peak between about 0.15 and 0.4 g. “the fuels exhibit a maximum in their flammability behavior in the partial-gravity range.” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)
  • New hazards: Dormancy, higher O₂, partial gravity and surface dust. “extended durations, dormancy intervals, increased oxygen concentrations, partial gravity conditions and the presence of surface dust. All of these changes can have significant impacts on fire safety system design and operations.” — Spacecraft Fire Safety Technology Development Plan for Exploration Missions (NTRS 20205000063)

Transit specifics (applies to: transit)

  • Self-reliance: Less suppressant, delayed contact with Earth. “Stores of suppressant and atmospheric diluents are more limited, long missions imply more accumulated wastes and possible relaxation of crew vigilance” — Friedman, R. (2000) Progress in Fire Detection and Suppression Technology for Future Space Missions, NASA/TM-2000-210337 (NTRS 20000120278)

Data & Model

The 144-row NASA flame-spread dataset with quotes and the honest model card: cross-validation, per-gravity accuracy, confusion matrix.

Model and data

  • Dataset: 144 real flame-spread experiments transcribed from 13 NASA reports (NTRS), each with a verbatim quote and page reference; by gravity: 0 g: 124, 0.165 g: 8, 0.38 g: 6, 1 g: 6.
  • Model: sklearn.ensemble.GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_depth=2, learning_rate=0.1); features oxygen_pct, pressure_kpa, flow_cm_s, gravity_g, material, flow_direction.
  • Stratified 5-fold cross-validated accuracy 0.729 (balanced 0.646); repeated CV 0.725 ± 0.064; leave-reports-out 0.688; majority-class baseline 0.611.
  • Out-of-fold accuracy by gravity: 0 g 0.798 (n=124), 0.165 g 0.375 (n=8), 0.38 g 0.333 (n=6), 1 g 0.167 (n=6). Partial-gravity outputs rest on very few tests and are effectively lookups of the nearest published test.
  • Confusion matrix (out-of-fold; rows = true no_spread, marginal_spread, spread): [[13, 5, 14], [6, 16, 2], [10, 2, 76]].
  • Range guard: no prediction is returned for a material/gravity combination, oxygen, pressure, airflow or flow direction outside the tested envelope, or for gas mixes other than O2/N2.
  • Separate real dataset: FLEX (PSI-69) experimental table, 274 droplet-combustion tests, 123 with added CO2 — shown as published, not used by the classifier.
  • Ask IGNITE-AI: retrieval over 1501 passages (NTRS abstracts, PSI metadata and tables, experiment rows, NASA pages) with TF-IDF; answers are verbatim quotes with source links; declines when nothing relevant is found.

AI-use disclosure

AI coding assistants helped write the software; all data values were transcribed from and checked against the cited NASA documents. No AI system produced any training value. No paid or cloud AI API is used at runtime: predictions come from a scikit-learn model, explanations are deterministic templates, and Ask IGNITE-AI quotes retrieved passages verbatim. Optional local Ollama generation is off by default and its output is rejected if it contains numbers not in the retrieved text.
